title_en: The lifespan of mind and matter

sources_read.markers: Book 1, ch. 4 (වීථි සංග්‍රහ විභාගය), pdf 315–316 / printed 305–306; extract cut from mid-page pdf 315 to mid-page pdf 316
Section headed '2. පරමාර්ථ ධර්මයන්ගේ ආයුෂ'; no page markers in extract

summary_en: Every mind-moment has three phases: arising, standing and dissolving. Together these make one 'mind-moment', which is the whole lifespan of a mind. Margaya says the three phases are equal and that a mind-moment is less than a hundred-thousandth of an eye-blink. Material phenomena last seventeen mind-moments, or fifty-one sub-moments: their arising and dissolving each take one sub-moment, like a mind's, and their standing phase stretches across forty-nine. Pradeepika notes that 22 of the 28 kinds of matter have this lifespan and six have less. Margaya explains why objects seem to last for months and years although their smallest units last only seventeen mind-moments: things are clusters of countless tiny units that do not all break at once and are continually replaced. Pradeepika also distinguishes minds within a process from the process-free minds (rebirth, life-continuum and death).

sinhala_explanation.heading: වීථි සිත් සහ වීථිමුක්ත සිත් (ප්‍රදීපිකාව)
sinhala_explanation.text: චිත්ත වීථියක් දක්වන විට සිත් දෙකොටසක් හමුවේ. මේ භවයේ සදොරින් ගත් අරමුණු එල්බගෙන උපදින සිත් 'වීථි සිත්' ය. පෙර භවයේ ගත් කර්ම, කර්ම නිමිත්ත, ගති නිමිත්ත යන අරමුණකින් එකක් එල්බගෙන පටිසන්ධි, භවඞ්ග, චුති කෘත්‍ය කරන ද්වාරවිමුක්ත සිත් වීථියට අයත් නොවන බැවින් 'වීථිමුක්ත සිත්' ය [C039-P:L23]. ද්වාර පහේ වීථි 'පඤ්චද්වාර වීථි' ලෙසද, ඒවාම 'චක්බු විඤ්ඤාණ වීථි' ආදි ලෙසද හැඳින්වේ [C039-P:L33].

sinhala_explanation.heading: චිත්තක්ෂණය: උත්පාද, ස්ථිති, භඞ්ග
sinhala_explanation.text: සිතට කුඩා ක්ෂණ තුනක් ඇත: උපදින අවස්ථාව උත්පාදක්ෂණය, පවතින අවස්ථාව ස්ථිතික්ෂණය (ඨිතික්ෂණය), බිඳෙන අවස්ථාව භඞ්ගක්ෂණය [C039-P:L25–L29; C039-M:L3]. මේ තුන එක්වූ විට එක් චිත්තක්ෂණයක් වේ; එයම සිතේ ආයුෂයයි [C039-P:L29; C039-M:L3]. මාර්ගය අනුව සිත යම් කාලයකින් උපදී නම් එපමණම කාලයක් පවතී, එපමණම කාලයකින් නිරුද්ධ වේ; ක්ෂණ තුනේ ප්‍රමාණයන් අඩු වැඩි නැත [C039-M:L3]. චිත්තක්ෂණය ඇසිපිය හෙළන කාලයෙන් ලක්ෂයෙන් පංගුවක් පමණවත් නොවන ඉතා කෙටි කාලයකි; මෙය තේරුම් ගැනීමට කලක් ගතවිය හැකි බවද මාර්ගය කියයි [C039-M:L3]. මේ ආයුෂ දැනගැනීම චිත්ත වීථි උගන්නා කෙනෙකු මුලින්ම කළ යුත්තකි [C039-M:L3].

sinhala_explanation.heading: රූපයේ ආයුෂ: චිත්තක්ෂණ 17 යි, කුඩා ක්ෂණ 51 යි
sinhala_explanation.text: සිතට ගෝචර වන රූප ධර්මයන්ට චිත්තක්ෂණ 17 ක්, එනම් කුඩා ක්ෂණ 51 ක් ආයුෂ ඇත [C039-P:L31; C039-M:L5]. රූපයටද උත්පාද, ස්ථිති, භඞ්ග අවස්ථා තුනක් ඇත; රූපයේ උත්පාදය හා භඞ්ගය සිතේ උත්පාදක්ෂණයට හා භඞ්ගක්ෂණයට සමාන කාලයකි; එහෙත් සිතේ ස්ථිතිය එක් කුඩා ක්ෂණයක් වන අතර රූපයේ ස්ථිතිය කුඩා ක්ෂණ 49 කි [C039-P:L31; C039-M:L5]. එබැවින් සිතේ මෙන් රූපයේ ක්ෂණ තුන සමාන නැත; රූපයේ ස්ථිතිය දිගය [C039-M:L5]. ප්‍රදීපිකාවට අනුව රූප 28 අතුරෙන් 22 කට චිත්තක්ෂණ 17 බැගින් ආයු ඇත; උපචය, සන්තති, ජරතා, අනිච්චතා, කාය විඤ්ඤත්ති, වචී විඤ්ඤත්ති යන රූප සයට ආයුෂ ඊට අඩුය; විස්තර රූප නිර්දේශයේ දැක්වේ [C039-P:L31]. මාර්ගය මේවා නම් නොකර 'චිත්තක්ෂණ 17 ක ආයුෂ නැති අප්‍රධාන රූප කීපයක්' ලෙස පමණක් සඳහන් කරයි [C039-M:L5].

sinhala_explanation.heading: වස්තු මාස ගණන් පවතින සේ පෙනෙන්නේ ඇයි (මාර්ගය)
sinhala_explanation.text: මාස, අවුරුදු ගණන් පවතින වස්තු දකින අයට රූපයක ආයුෂ චිත්තක්ෂණ 17 යැයි පිළිගැනීම අපහසු විය හැක [C039-M:L7]. දුර සිට එකක් සේ පෙනෙන වැලි ගොඩ වැලි කැට සමූහයක් සේම, අබ ඇටයක් වුවද කුඩා ද්‍රව්‍ය සමූහයකි; සියලු වස්තු රූප කලාපවලින් සෑදී ඇත; රූප කලාපයේ පරමායුෂ චිත්තක්ෂණ 17 කි; ඇසිපිය හෙළන කාලය තුළ රූප කලාප දහස් ගණනක් එකිනෙකට පසුව ඉපිද බිඳේ; අබ ඇටයක් පමණ වස්තුවක රූප කලාප කෝටි ගණනක් ඇත [C039-M:L9]. වස්තුවල වෙනසක් නොපෙනෙන්නේ කරුණු දෙකක් නිසාය: එක් වස්තුවක රූප කලාප සියල්ල එකවර නොබිඳීම, සහ බිඳෙන කලාප වෙනුවට එම තැන්වලම අලුත් කලාප පහළ වීම [C039-M:L9]. එක් වස්තුවක සෑම ක්ෂණයකටම (දෙවැන්නේ සිට) පැමිණි කලාප ලක්ෂ ගණනක් ඇති බැවින්, 51 වන ක්ෂණයේ කලාප බිඳෙන විට අනෙක් ක්ෂණවලට පැමිණි කලාප ඉතිරිව පවතී [C039-M:L11]. චිත්ත වීථියක් ඇතිවන්නේ එක් වස්තුවක ඇති වයසින් සමාන රූප සමූහයක් අරමුණු කරගෙනය; වයසින් නොයෙක් ප්‍රමාණ වූ සියලු රූප ගැන එකවර වීථි ඇති නොවේ [C039-M:L13].

key_terms.en: mind-moment; the lifespan of one mind
cluster of material phenomena; the smallest unit things are built from
growth, continuity, decay, impermanence (characteristic kinds of matter)
key_terms.note: among the six with a shorter lifespan per Pradeepika
among the six with a shorter lifespan per Pradeepika

human_interpretation_en.heading: Everything solid is quietly being replaced
human_interpretation_en.text: In this picture, the table, the wall and your own hand are like a sand heap seen from a distance: countless tiny parts, each lasting only an instant. Nothing seems to change because the parts do not all go at once, and each one that goes is replaced in the same spot. Stability, then, is not stillness. It is constant, well-timed renewal.

human_interpretation_en.heading: The mind is quicker than the world it knows
human_interpretation_en.text: A single moment of mind comes and goes far faster than the physical things it knows. Matter lingers about seventeen times longer, just long enough for one full pass of perceiving to catch it. Put simply, the world holds still for exactly as long as it takes to be noticed once.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Three beats in everything
human_interpretation_en.text: Mind and matter share one rhythm: a thing comes up, it stays, it breaks. They differ only in how long the middle beat lasts. For thoughts it is as short as the other two; for material things it is drawn out. The idea gives a simple, unsentimental way to look at change: every presence has a beginning, a middle and an end, however short.

does_not_transfer: The source's statement is technical measurement, not an 'everything is impermanent, so let go' exhortation. Neither extract draws a moral here.

The material clusters are not atoms, molecules or cells, and seventeen mind-moments is not a duration that can be measured in seconds. Margaya's 'less than a hundred-thousandth of a blink' is an image, not a figure to quote as science. Presenting it as physics or cell turnover would distort it.
'Live in the moment' misreads it. The 'moment' here is far below anything a person can experience or dwell in.
The replacement argument explains why things look unchanged. It is not a 'you are a new person every seven years' factoid, and it should not be paired with one.

story_seeds.seed: Masons repoint an old temple wall or stupa base brick by brick, so that it remains 'the same wall'.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Old bricks cut out, lime mortar mixed, new bricks matched and set, and the wall seen from a distance where no change is visible. The masons discuss how much of the original is left.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: It is a real-world version of Margaya's argument: a thing seems unchanged because its parts are replaced one at a time, never all at once.
story_seeds.setting_type: Old village temple or ancient monument under conservation
story_seeds.risk: Heritage sites can be politically and religiously sensitive, and filming may need permits. It should not become a lecture on impermanence set over a restoration montage.

story_seeds.seed: Salt workers rake and gather salt in shallow pans where brine evaporates and crystals re-form every few days.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Flooding of the pans, crystals forming at the edges, raking into heaps, carrying baskets, the heaps dissolving at the edges in rain, and the cycle repeating through the season.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Arising, standing and breaking are visible here as a working cycle. A salt heap is also a close cousin of Margaya's sand heap: one shape made of countless grains.
story_seeds.setting_type: Coastal salt pans in the dry zone
story_seeds.risk: Time-lapse cliché. The workers' pay and conditions should not be aestheticised away.

story_seeds.seed: A watch-repairer in a small-town shop works among dozens of ticking clocks.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: A loupe, tiny gears, balance wheels, the ticking of many clocks slightly out of step, customers collecting heirlooms, and the repairer's talk about the smallest units of time his tools can see.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The film can bring out, without saying it, the gap between the smallest time human tools can mark and the far smaller 'moment' of the source.
story_seeds.setting_type: Small watch and clock repair shop in a market town
story_seeds.risk: Forcing a clock metaphor. The repairer's own life and craft must be worth the film.

story_seeds.seed: A hand sifter at a building site sieves river sand into a fine heap for plastering.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Shovelling onto a tilted mesh, grains pouring through, the stones left behind, and the heap growing into one smooth shape. The worker talks about the quality of sand.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: It is Margaya's own image made literal: a heap that looks like one thing is countless separate grains.
story_seeds.setting_type: House construction site in a village or town
story_seeds.risk: Too literal. River sand also connects to contested sand-mining issues that should not be dropped in casually or ignored if they arise.

cross_source_notes: Both sources agree that matter lasts 17 mind-moments, or 51 sub-moments, with a standing phase of 49 sub-moments and arising and dissolution equal to a mind's [C039-P:L31; C039-M:L5].
Margaya states explicitly that the three sub-moments of a mind are equal [C039-M:L3]. Pradeepika implies this by saying that the standing time of mental phenomena is one sub-moment [C039-P:L31].

Pradeepika names the six kinds of matter with shorter lifespans and gives a count of 22 of 28 with the full lifespan [C039-P:L31]. Margaya says only that 'a few minor kinds of matter' lack the 17-moment lifespan [C039-M:L5].

Only Margaya gives the eye-blink comparison, the sand-heap and mustard-seed images, the replacement explanation and the point that a process takes as its object a group of equally-aged matter [C039-M:L3–L13].
Only Pradeepika gives the distinction between process minds and process-free minds and the naming of the five sense-door processes [C039-P:L23; C039-P:L33].

Terminology: Pradeepika writes ඨීතික්ෂණය, Margaya ස්ථිතික්ෂණය. The images of speed also differ: C034-P L37 speaks of 'lakhs of crores' of minds in a finger-snap, while Margaya speaks of a mind-moment as less than a hundred-thousandth of an eye-blink [C039-M:L3].
uncertainties: C039-M L11 says that when matter at the 51st sub-moment breaks, the clusters at the '2nd to 49th' sub-moments remain. By its own logic this should arguably be the 1st (or 2nd) to 50th. It may be a slip in the source or in transcription. It is not corrected here.
C039-M L11 'ලක්ෂණ ගණනක්' is presumably ලක්ෂ ගණනක් ('lakhs'). This is likely OCR.

Pradeepika's list of six kinds of matter with shorter lifespans [C039-P:L31] defers details to the matter chapter, which was not read. Exactly how their lifespans differ, particularly for the four characteristics such as growth and decay, needs an expert check.

Whether a mind has a distinct standing phase at all is a point some Abhidhamma commentators have debated. These sources treat it as settled, and an expert should confirm before scripts state it flatly. This is flagged, not resolved.
The Pradeepika extract is cut mid-page at both ends [C039-P:L12], and the five-door process discussion continues in the next concept.
